# AF 第九章 原文（重制基线）

## Chapter 9

[P01] Boxer's split（分裂） hoof took a long time to heal（治愈）. They had started to rebuild the windmill（风车） the day after the victory celebrations（庆祝） ended. Boxer refused to take even one day off, and he made it a point of honour not to let anyone see his pain. In the evenings he would admit（承认） privately（私下地） to Clover that the hoof troubled him a great deal. Clover treated the hoof with poultices（药膏） of herbs（草药） which she made by chewing（咀嚼） them, and both she and Benjamin urged（催促） Boxer to work less hard. "A horse's lungs（肺） do not last for ever," she said to him. But Boxer would not listen.

[P02] He had, he said, only one real ambition left--to see the windmill well started before he reached the age for retirement（退休）. At the beginning, when the laws of Animal Farm were first made, the retiring（退休） age had been fixed for horses and pigs at twelve, for cows at fourteen, for dogs at nine, for sheep at seven, and for hens and geese at five. Liberal（开明的） old-age pensions（养老金） had been agreed upon. As yet no animal had actually retired（退休的） on pension（养老金）, but lately the subject had been discussed more and more. Now that the small field beyond the orchard（果园） had been set aside（旁边） for barley（大麦）, it was said that a corner of the large pasture（牧场） was to be fenced off and turned into a grass-ground for old animals to eat.

[P03] For a horse, it was said, the pension would be five pounds of corn a day and, in winter, fifteen pounds of hay（干草）, with a carrot or maybe an apple on public holidays. Boxer's twelfth birthday was due（由于） in the late summer of the following year. Meanwhile（同时） life was hard. The winter was as cold as the last one, and food was even shorter. Once again all rations（配给） were cut, except those of the pigs and the dogs. Squealer explained that too strict equality（平等） in rations would go against the principles（原则） of Animalism（动物主义）. In any case he had no trouble proving to the other animals that they were NOT really short of food, whatever appearances might be.

[P04] For the time being, of course, they had found it necessary to make a "readjustment（调整）," as Squealer always called it.of rations (Squealer always called it a "readjustment," never a "reduction（减少）"), but compared with the days of Jones, the improvement was great. Reading out the figures in a shrill（尖锐的）, quick voice, he proved to them in detail that they had more oats（燕麦）, more hay, more turnips（萝卜） than in Jones's day, that they worked shorter hours, that their drinking water was better, that they lived longer, that more of their young ones lived past infancy（婴儿期）, and that they had more straw（稻草） in their stalls（畜栏） and suffered less from fleas（跳蚤）.

[P05] The animals believed every single word of it. To tell the truth, Jones and everything he stood for had almost faded（褪色） out of their memories. They knew that life these days was hard and bare（仅够）, that they were often hungry and often cold, and that they were usually working whenever they were not asleep. But without doubt things had been worse in the old days. They were glad to believe this was so. Besides, back then they had been slaves and now they were free, and that made all the difference, just as Squealer never failed to point out.

[P06] In the autumn the four sows（母猪） all gave birth at about the same time, producing thirty-one young pigs between them. The young pigs were piebald（花斑）, and since Napoleon was the only boar（公猪） on the farm, it was easy to guess who their father was. It was announced that later, when bricks（砖块） and timber（木材） had been bought, a schoolroom（教室） would be built in the farmhouse（农舍） garden. For now, the young pigs were taught by Napoleon himself in the farmhouse kitchen. They took their exercise in the garden, and were told not to play with the other young animals. About this time, too, it was made a rule that when a pig and any other animal met on the path（小路）, the other animal must stand aside: and also that all pigs, of whatever degree, were to have the right to wear green ribbons（丝带） on their tails on Sundays. The farm had had a fairly good year, but was still short of money.

[P07] There were the bricks, sand, and lime（石灰） to buy for the schoolroom, and they also needed to save again for the windmill machinery（机器）. Then there were lamp oil and candles for the house, sugar for Napoleon's own table (he stopped the other pigs from having it, because he said it made them fat), and all the usual replacements（替换品） such as tools, nails（钉子）, string, coal, wire（电线）, scrap（废料）-iron, and dog biscuits. A stump（树桩） of hay and part of the potato crop were sold off, and the egg contract was raised to six hundred a week, so that year the hens barely（几乎不） hatched（孵化） enough chicks to keep their numbers the same.

[P08] Rations, cut in December, were cut again in February, and lanterns in the stalls were banned（禁止） to save oil. But the pigs seemed comfortable enough, and were even putting on weight. One afternoon in late February a warm, rich, tasty（美味） smell, such as the animals had never smelt before, came across the yard from the little brew（酿造）-house, unused（未使用的） in Jones's time, which stood beyond the kitchen. Someone said it was the smell of cooking barley. The animals sniffed（嗅） the air hungrily（饥饿地） and wondered whether a warm mash（糊状饲料） was being made for their supper. But no warm mash appeared, and on the following Sunday it was announced that from then on all barley would be kept for the pigs.

[P09] The field beyond the orchard had already been sown（播种） with barley. And the news soon spread that every pig was now getting a ration（配给） of a pint（品脱） of beer daily, which is 1/8 of a gallon（加仑） or 0.568 liters（升）, with half a gallon for Napoleon himself, which was always served to him in the Crown（王冠） Derby（德比） soup tureen（大碗）. But if there were hardships（苦难） to be borne（承受）, they were partly（部分地） offset（抵消） by the fact that life nowadays had a greater dignity（尊严） than it had had before. There were more songs, more speeches, more processions（游行队伍）. Napoleon had commanded（命令） that once a week there should be held something called a Spontaneous（自发的） Demonstration（示范）, the object of which was to celebrate the struggles（斗争） and triumphs（胜利） of Animal Farm.

[P10] At the set time the animals would leave work and march round the farm in military（军事） formation（形成）, pigs first, then horses, cows, sheep, and chickens and other birds. The dogs walked beside the procession（游行）, and at the front marched Napoleon's black cockerel（小公鸡）. Boxer and Clover always carried between them a green banner（横幅） marked with the hoof and the horn and the words, "Long live Comrade（同志） Napoleon!" After that came poems recited in Napoleon's honour, and a speech by Squealer on the latest rises in food production, and sometimes a shot from the gun.

[P11] The sheep were the greatest devotees（爱好者） of the Spontaneous Demonstration, and if anyone complained (as a few animals sometimes did, when no pigs or dogs were near) that they wasted time and that meant a lot of standing about in the cold, the sheep were sure to silence him with a tremendous（极大的） bleating of "Four legs good, two legs bad!" But mostly（大多数） the animals enjoyed these celebrations. They found it comforting to be reminded that, after all, they were truly their own masters and that the work they did was for their own good. So that, what with the songs, the processions, Squealer's lists of figures, the thunder of the gun, the crowing（啼叫） of the cockerel, and the fluttering（飘动） of the flag, they were able to forget that their bellies（腹部） were empty（空的）, at least part of the time. In April, Animal Farm was proclaimed（宣布） a Republic（共和国）, and it became necessary to elect（选举） a President.

[P12] There was only one candidate（候选人）, Napoleon, and everyone voted for him. On the same day, people said that new papers had been found which showed more details about Snowball working with Jones. It now seemed that Snowball had not just tried to lose the Battle of the Cowshed（牛棚） by a trick, as the animals had thought before, but had openly（公开地） fought on Jones's side. In fact, he had been the leader of the human forces, and had rushed into battle with the words "Long live Humanity（人类）!" on his lips（嘴唇）. The wounds on Snowball's back, which a few of the animals still remembered seeing, had been made by Napoleon's teeth.

[P13] He was quite the same as before, still did no work, and talked in the same way as ever about Sugarcandy（糖块） Mountain. He would sit on a stump, flap（拍打） his black wings, and talk for hours to anyone who would listen. "Up there, comrades（同志们）," he would say seriously, pointing to the sky with his big beak（鸟嘴）--"up there, just on the other side of that dark cloud--there it lies, Sugarcandy Mountain, that happy country where we poor animals shall rest for ever from our labours!" He even said he had been there on one of his higher flights, and had seen the everlasting（永恒的） fields of clover and the linseed（亚麻籽） cake and lump（块） sugar growing on the hedges（树篱）.

[P14] Many of the animals believed him. Their lives, they reasoned, were hungry and full of labour（劳作）; was it not right and just that a better world should exist（存在） somewhere else? What was hard to determine（决定） was the attitude（态度） of the pigs towards Moses. They declared（宣布） contemptuously（轻蔑地） that his stories about Sugarcandy Mountain were lies, yet they let him stay on the farm, not working, with a gill（鳃） of beer a day.

After his hoof（蹄） had healed（治愈） up, Boxer worked harder than ever. Indeed, all the animals worked like slaves that year. Apart（分开） from the regular work of the farm, and the rebuilding of the windmill, there was the schoolhouse（校舍） for the young pigs, started in March.

[P15] Sometimes the long hours with too little food were hard to bear, but Boxer never gave up. In nothing he said or did was there any sign that his strength had gone. Only his hide was less shiny（闪亮）, and his great haunches（臀部） seemed to have shrunken（萎缩）. The others said, "Boxer will pick up when the spring grass comes on"; but the spring came and Boxer grew no fatter. Sometimes on the slope（斜坡） up to the quarry（采石场） top, when he braced（撑住） his muscles（肌肉） against a huge boulder（巨石）, it seemed that only the will to go on kept him on his feet.

[P16] At such times his lips formed the words, "I will work harder"; he had no voice left. Once again Clover and Benjamin warned him to take care of his health, but Boxer paid no attention. His twelfth birthday was coming near. He did not care what happened so long as a good store of stone（石头） was piled up before he went on pension. Late one evening in the summer, a sudden rumour（谣言） ran round the farm that something had happened to Boxer. He had gone out alone to drag（拖） a load（负载） of stone down to the windmill. And sure enough, the rumour was true. A few minutes later two pigeons came racing in with the news; "Boxer has fallen!

[P17] He is lying（躺） on his side and can't（不能） get up!" About half the animals rushed to the knoll（小丘） where the windmill stood. There lay Boxer, between the shafts（车辕） of the cart, his neck stretched（伸展） out, unable（无法） to lift his head. His eyes were glassy（玻璃般）, his sides wet with sweat（汗水）. A thin stream of blood ran out of his mouth. Clover fell to her knees beside him. "Boxer!" she cried, "how are you?" "It is my lung（肺）," said Boxer weakly（虚弱地）. "It does not matter. You will finish the windmill without me.

[P18] There is a good store of stone accumulated（积累）. I had only another month to go anyway. To tell you the truth, I had been looking forward to my retirement. And perhaps, as Benjamin is growing old too, they will let him retire（退休） at the same time and be a companion（同伴） to me." "We must get help at once," said Clover. "Run, somebody, and tell Squealer what has happened." All the other animals raced back to the farmhouse to run and give Squealer the news. Only Clover remained, and Benjamin who lay down at Boxer's side, and, without speaking, kept the flies off him with his long tail.

[P19] After about a quarter of an hour Squealer appeared, full of sympathy（同情）. He said Comrade Napoleon had learned with deep distress（痛苦） of this misfortune（不幸） to one of the most loyal（忠诚） workers, and was making arrangements（安排） to send Boxer to the hospital at Willingdon. The animals felt uneasy（不安）. Except for Mollie and Snowball, no other animal had ever left the farm, and they did not like to think of their sick comrade in the hands of human beings. However, Squealer easily convinced（确信） them that the veterinary（兽医的） surgeon（外科医生） in Willingdon could treat Boxer's case better than on the farm.

[P20] About half an hour later, when Boxer had recovered（恢复） somewhat（有点）, he got to his feet with difficulty and limped（跛行） back to his stall（畜栏）, where Clover and Benjamin had made a good bed of straw. For two days Boxer stayed there. The pigs sent a large bottle of pink medicine from the bathroom chest, and Clover gave it to Boxer twice a day after meals. In the evenings she lay in his stall and talked to him, while Benjamin kept the flies off. Boxer said he was not sorry for what had happened.

[P21] If he got well again, he might live another three years, and he looked forward to the peaceful（平静） days in the corner of the big pasture. It would be the first time he had fun to study and improve his mind. He said he wanted to give the rest of his life to learning the other twenty-two letters of the alphabet（字母表）. However, Benjamin and Clover could only be with Boxer after work, and it was in the middle of the day when the van（货车） came to take him away. The animals were all at work pulling up turnips under a pig's eye, when they were surprised to see Benjamin come running（跑步） from the farm buildings, crying out at the top of his voice.

[P22] It was the first time they had seen Benjamin excited—the first time anyone had seen him run fast. "Quick, quick!" he shouted. "Come now! They're（他们是） taking Boxer away!" Without waiting for orders from the pig, the animals stopped work and ran back to the farm buildings. Sure enough, there in the yard was a large closed van, pulled by two horses, with letters on its side and a clever-looking man in a low-crowned（加冕） bowler hat on the driver's seat. And Boxer's stall was empty. The animals crowded round the van. "Good-bye, Boxer!" they said together, "good-bye!" "Fools! Fools!" shouted Benjamin, jumping round them and hitting（击打） the earth with his small hoofs（蹄）.

[P23] "Fools! Do you not see what is written on the side of that van?" That gave the animals pause（暂停）, and there was a hush（寂静）. Muriel began to spell out the words. But Benjamin pushed her aside and in the middle of a deadly silence he read: "'Alfred（阿尔弗雷德） Simmonds（西蒙兹）, Horse Slaughterer（屠夫） and Glue Boiler, Willingdon. Dealer in Hides and Bone-Meal. Kennels（狗舍） Supplied.' Do you not understand what that means? They are taking Boxer to the knacker（屠夫）'s!" A cry of horror（恐怖） burst（爆发） from all the animals. At this moment the man on the box whipped up his horses and the van moved out of the yard at a smart trot（疾走）.

[P24] All the animals followed, shouting as loud as they could. Clover pushed her way to the front. The van began to go faster, and Clover got to a canter（慢跑）. "Boxer!" she cried. "Boxer! Boxer!" Just then, as if he had heard the noise, Boxer's face, with the white stripe（条纹） down his nose, showed at the small window at the back of the van. "Boxer!" cried Clover in a terrible voice. "Get out! Get out quickly! They're taking you to your death!" All the animals took up the cry of "Get out, Boxer, get out!" But the van was already pulling away from them.

[P25] It was not sure whether Boxer had understood what Clover said. But a moment later his face went from the window and there was a sound of a tremendous（极大的） drumming（击鼓） of hoofs inside the van. He was trying to kick his way out. Once a few kicks from Boxer would have broken the van into matchwood（火柴棍）. But alas（唉）! his strength had gone; and in a few moments the sound of drumming hoofs grew fainter（更微弱） and died away. In despair（绝望） the animals called on the two horses which pulled the van to stop. "Comrades, comrades!" they shouted. "Don't（不） take your own brother to his death!" But the stupid brutes（畜生）, too silly to understand, only put back their ears and went faster.

[P26] Boxer's face did not come back at the window. It was too late when someone thought of racing ahead to shut the five-barred（阻挡） gate; but in another moment the van went through it and was quickly disappearing down the road. Boxer was never seen again. Three days later, people said he had died in the hospital at Willingdon, although he had received every attention a horse could have. Squealer came to tell the news. He had, he said, been there during Boxer's last hours. "It was the most affecting（感人的） sight I have ever seen!" said Squealer, lifting his trotter（猪蹄） and wiping（擦拭） away a tear. "I was at his bedside（床边） at the very last.

[P27] Almost too weak to speak, he whispered（低语） that his only sadness was to die before the windmill was finished. 'Forward, comrades! Forward in the name of the uprising（起义）. Long live Animal Farm! Long live Comrade Napoleon! Napoleon is always right.' Those were his last words, comrades." Here Squealer's demeanour（举止） suddenly changed. Then Squealer changed. He fell silent, his little eyes darting（飞奔） suspicious（可疑的） looks from side to side before he went on. He said a foolish and wicked（邪恶的） rumour had been spread when Boxer was taken away.

[P28] Some of the animals had noticed that the van which took Boxer away was marked "Horse Slaughterer," and had really jumped to the conclusion that Boxer was being sent to the knacker's. Squealer said it was almost unbelievable（难以置信） that any animal could be so stupid. Surely, he cried angrily（愤怒地）, whisking（搅拌） his tail and skipping（跳跃） from side to side, surely they knew their beloved（心爱的） Leader, Comrade Napoleon, better than that? But the explanation was really very simple. The van had before been the property（财产） of the knacker, and had been bought by the veterinary surgeon, who had not yet painted the old name out. That was how the mistake had arisen. The animals were very relieved（松了一口气） to hear this.

[P29] And when Squealer went on to give more details of Boxer's death-bed, the good care he had received, and the costly（昂贵的） medicines Napoleon had paid for without a thought about the cost, their last doubts went away and their sorrow（悲伤） for their comrade's death was eased by the thought that at least he had died happy. Napoleon himself came to the meeting on the following Sunday morning and made a short speech in Boxer's honour. He said it had not been possible to bring back their lamented（哀悼） comrade's remains for burial（埋葬） on the farm, but he had ordered a large wreath（花圈） made from the laurels（月桂） in the farmhouse garden and sent down to be placed on Boxer's grave（坟墓）.

[P30] And in a few days' time the pigs planned to hold a memorial（纪念碑） banquet（宴会） in Boxer's honour. Napoleon ended his speech with a reminder of Boxer's two favourite maxims（格言）, "I will work harder" and "Comrade Napoleon is always right" -- maxims, he said, which every animal would do well to adopt（收养） as his own. On the day set for the banquet, a grocer（杂货商）'s van drove up from Willingdon and delivered（递送） a large wooden crate（板条箱） at the farmhouse. That night there was the sound of loud singing, which was followed by what sounded like a violent（暴力的） quarrel（争吵） and ended at about eleven o'clock with a tremendous（极大的） crash（碰撞） of glass. No one moved in the farmhouse before noon on the following day, and the word went round that from somewhere or other the pigs had got the money to buy themselves another case of whisky（威士忌）.
